title: The Black Death, 1346–1353
intro: The Black Death was the plague pandemic that crossed western Eurasia and North Africa between 1346 and 1353, the deadliest in recorded history. It was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of rats and other animals and, in its pneumonic form, from person to person. First reported among the Golden Horde and at the besieged Genoese port of Caffa in the Crimea, it moved along the sea lanes of Italian merchants to Constantinople, Sicily and Egypt, then inland along roads and rivers until it had reached Scandinavia and Russia. This map follows it half a year at a time, marking the towns where the sources date an outbreak; the shaded areas are schematic outlines drawn around those towns.
outcome: Between a quarter and well over half of Europe's people died, and about a third of the Middle East's; the plague returned every few years for centuries.
uncertainty: Where the pandemic began is disputed. Tombstones near Lake Issyk-Kul record a 'pestilence' in 1338–1339 and ancient DNA from them carries the ancestral strain, but others place the source on the steppe north-west of the Caspian or further west. The story of corpses catapulted into Caffa rests on one writer who was not there. The ships' tracks drawn here are inferred from the ports they linked, and the shaded regions are hulls around documented outbreaks, not the true extent: some areas inside them were spared or lightly hit, and regional mortality varied widely. Dates for the Levant differ between accounts (some give 1347), and death tolls for single cities are estimates.

steps.title: Plague in the Horde and at Caffa
steps.narrative: Russian chronicles record a great pestilence in 1346 among the Tatars and the other peoples of the Golden Horde, in its towns on the lower Volga. That year Khan Jani Beg's army was besieging Caffa, the walled Genoese trading colony on the Crimean coast, and the disease broke out among the besiegers. The Piacenza notary Gabriele de' Mussi, writing soon afterwards, claimed the Tatars catapulted their dead over the walls; whether or not they did, rats and fleas could cross siege lines on their own, and the town was infected.

steps.title: Ships carry it to Constantinople
steps.narrative: Genoese merchants escaping the Black Sea took the infection with them, and by the summer of 1347 it had reached Constantinople. The co-emperor John VI Kantakouzenos lost his thirteen-year-old son Andronikos to it and later wrote an account modelled on Thucydides' plague of Athens, remarking that it travelled by ship from one sea city to the next. The first outbreak in the capital went on for about a year.

steps.title: Messina and Alexandria
steps.narrative: In October 1347 twelve Genoese galleys put in at Messina in Sicily with sick and dying crews. The Messinese drove them out of the harbour, but too late: within weeks the disease was all over the island. That same autumn a merchant ship carrying slaves from Constantinople brought it to Alexandria, the great port of Mamluk Egypt. From these two footholds it would move into Italy, North Africa and the Levant.

steps.title: Into Italy and up the Rhône
steps.narrative: Galleys from the east reached Genoa and Venice in January 1348, but it was Pisa, struck a few weeks later, that opened the way into inland Tuscany. Towards the end of January a galley turned away from Italy brought the plague to Marseille, and it moved up the Rhône to Avignon, then the seat of the papacy. Pope Clement VI stayed in the city, and his physician Guy de Chauliac described two forms of the disease: a fever with coughing of blood, and the swellings in the armpit and groin.

steps.title: Tuscany, Tunis and the road to Paris
steps.narrative: Through the spring of 1348 the plague swept Tuscany. Florence, home to perhaps 110,000 to 120,000 people a decade earlier, had about 50,000 by 1351, and Boccaccio set the storytellers of the Decameron in this year. In Siena the chronicler Agnolo di Tura wrote that he buried his five children himself. A ship from Sicily infected Tunis in April. By June the disease had crossed France to Paris and reached the ports of Aragon, and a ship had landed it at Melcombe in Dorset, its first foothold in England.

steps.title: Cairo, Syria, Paris and London
steps.narrative: In the second half of 1348 the plague reached Cairo, the largest city of the Mediterranean world. The boy sultan an-Nasir Hasan left the city, and between a third and two-fifths of its people died within eight months. Damascus was struck in July and Aleppo in October, and pilgrims carried it to Mecca. In the west Paris lost about half of its inhabitants, London was reached by the end of the year and Dublin earlier in the autumn. From Avignon, Clement VI condemned those who blamed the Jews, pointing out that Jews were dying too.

steps.title: The German lands and the pogroms
steps.narrative: In 1349 the epidemic spread across the German lands. Fear turned on the Jews, who were accused of poisoning wells: in Strasbourg about 2,000 were murdered in February, before the plague had even reached the town. Bands of flagellants went from town to town, whipping themselves in public penance. Vienna and the Rhineland were struck, and in England the disease worked north from the southern ports.

steps.title: A ship to Norway
steps.narrative: In 1349 a ship arriving at Askøy, outside Bergen, brought the plague to Norway, and it spread from there into the country. In August the Jewish communities of Mainz and Cologne were destroyed. By the end of the year the disease was in Scotland, carried north from England, and it was moving on through the German and Low Countries towns.

steps.title: The North Sea and the Baltic
steps.narrative: In 1350 the plague swept the North Sea and Baltic coasts. At least three in five people may have died in Hamburg and Bremen, and Lübeck, Denmark and Sweden were struck in turn. Some regions were hit far less hard: the evidence of pollen from farmland suggests that farming in parts of central and eastern Europe carried on almost undisturbed, while Scandinavia, France, western Germany and central Italy show signs of heavy loss.

steps.title: Counting the dead
steps.narrative: By 1351 the first wave had passed through most of western Europe. Agents of Clement VI were said to have counted 23,840,000 dead in Christian Europe, about a third of its people, though modern estimates run from a quarter to well over half. Sixty large and 150 smaller Jewish communities had been destroyed, and many survivors moved east to Poland, where King Casimir the Great received them.

steps.title: Pskov and Novgorod
steps.narrative: In 1352 the plague reached the Russian lands from the west, striking Pskov and then Novgorod, the great trading republic whose market linked the Baltic to the Russian interior. Contemporary accounts describe a toll in the Russian towns much like that in western Europe.

steps.title: Moscow
steps.narrative: In 1353 the epidemic reached Moscow. Grand Prince Simeon the Proud died of it in April, and his young sons and his brother Andrei died in the same outbreak. With Moscow the first great wave of the second plague pandemic had run its course across Europe, though the disease would return every few years for generations.
